title: Elevenostat: Don't Believe the Label
body_text: I’m always glad to see articles like this one, where someone goes to the trouble of confirming whether “Compound X is a selective probe for Protein Target Y” is a true statement. That’s because it’s not all that easy to find a selective probe! A basic rule of small molecules in biological systems is “A lot of things bind to a lot of stuff” (speaking rigorously and quantitatively here, you understand), and there are many, many instances where people have found that a given compound’s biological activity is not only mediated by its putative target, but by something else entirely. The paper linked above details an even worse situation. The compound elevenostat has been treated as an HDAC11-selective probe for some time, but here the authors show that it only binds to that subtype rather weakly (10 micromolar or so). It’s a much better binder to HDAC6 and HDAC10 (single-digit nanomolar!), and its cellular activity is much more consistent with that sort of mechanism. So it looks like you can write off any HDAC11 papers that base any conclusions on elevenostat experiments. Getting HDAC selectivity for any particular isoform is not a walk in the park. I worked in that area years ago, and like most all the enzymes with a zinc atom in the active site, most of the tight-binding compounds are binding that way because they have a “zincophore” head group (hydroxamic acid, sulfonamide, benzamide and so on). There are plenty of these out there, but there are plenty of zinc-dependent enzyme active sites out there too, when you consider all the HDACs and all the matrix metalloproteases just to start with. Most of the time, selectivity tends to come more from the structure of the rest of the ligand bearing the zinc-binding head group, but some of those binding sites are hard to differentiate. But this is a pretty egregious case. Adding to the frustration is that the whistle had already been blown about elevenostat/HDAC11 back in 2019! But this latest paper has a whole series of references that used the compound for that purpose well after that article came out. If you search for elevenostat itself, most of the references from biochemical suppliers cheerfully list it as a selective HDAC11 inhibitor, which just goes to show you how much you should trust labels in this business. So, once again: look over those chemical probes yourself. See if anyone has actually run binding profiles on them and what the numbers are. Don’t just take everyone else’s word for it, especially not the word of the people who would like to sell you some. The misuse of chemical probes in assays has long been prevasive; there's no need to add to it. I've written about this it many times and I will no doubt write about it many more. But one can hope.
